commits.author: ch4mpy
commits.message:
Document what goes wrong without spring-addons, not only what it saves

The entry points (README, docs home, llms.txt, Maven descriptions) framed the
starters as a way to write less configuration, and readers, humans and coding
assistants alike, repeated that framing back and concluded "plain Spring
Security is enough for a simple API". The actual argument is that Spring
Security's OAuth2 defaults were designed for a browser doing navigations, and
that a backend consumed by a single-page or mobile application silently gets
several of them wrong: roles that never become authorities, preflights
rejected, a login flow a fetch cannot start, a CSRF token JavaScript cannot
read, an open redirect after login, random logouts under load, tests that
never run the real converter.

- New page docs/what-goes-wrong.md: symptom, Spring default, what it is
  (security flaw, broken behaviour, test that lies), property. States the
  honest boundary: Boot's resource server chain is a reasonable default, the
  starter keeps Spring's defaults unless a property says otherwise, a
  server-rendered application does not need any of this.
- README and docs home: new tagline and a "Why not just the official
  starters" table before the quickstart, a "when not to use it" paragraph,
  and a note that the migration guides overstate the churn (8.4.0, 8.5.0 and
  9.2.0 concern the REST starter only).
- docs/oidc/risks.md becomes "Risks, in both directions": the risks of the
  hand-written alternative next to the risks of the dependency.
- llms.txt: a section for assistants asked whether to recommend the library,
  with the decision criteria and the counter-case.
- Maven descriptions of the reactor and of spring-addons-starter-oidc.
- without-spring-addons.md: the CSRF row acknowledges csrf.spa() in Spring
  Security 7.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: ch4mpy
commits.message:
Add the two write-ups to the documentation site

Reference pages answer "how do I configure this". Neither of the two things
this repository does that nothing else does is a configuration question, and
both were only documented as a section inside a reference page, where nobody
looking for the problem would find them.

- "An OAuth2 BFF for a single-page application, end to end" walks the six
  Spring Security behaviours a JavaScript frontend needs which the defaults do
  not provide, because the defaults were designed for browser navigations: the
  401 instead of a login redirect, the 2xx with a Location header, the CSRF
  cookie the deferred token loading otherwise never writes, PKCE on a
  confidential client, validated post-login and post-logout destinations, and
  logout in both directions.
- "One refresh token flow at a time" states the defect the way a maintainer
  meets it, random 401s blamed on the session store, explains why declining it
  upstream was the right call, and lists what a cross-instance implementation
  has to get right for anyone who needs one.

Both are readable without taking the dependency, which is the point: they
document Spring Security problems, not this library.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: ch4mpy
commits.message:
Point the READMEs at the documentation site

Keeping the full reference in both the module READMEs and the site would put the
same text on two domains, which is the opposite of the reason the site exists:
the two pages would compete with each other for the same queries instead of one
of them ranking.

Each module README keeps what a visitor landing on the module needs, the pitch
in a paragraph and the dependency snippet, and links to the pages which now
carry the reference. Nothing is lost, the content moved in the previous commit
and git keeps the history.

The root README, `llms.txt`, the samples README and the release notes are
repointed at the pages which replaced the README sections they referenced,
including the anchors, which the section numbering used to make cryptic
(`#1-2-12` is now `/oidc/client/#concurrent-refresh-token-flows`).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: ch4mpy
commits.message:
Publish the documentation as a GitHub Pages site

The 923-line `spring-addons-starter-oidc` README is a good manual and a poor
search target: one page competing for thirty different queries, on a domain
which ranks the repository rather than the subject. `docs/` splits it, and the
other module READMEs, into one page per concern, each with its own URL, title
and description.

The site is Jekyll with the `just-the-docs` remote theme, served from this
folder by GitHub Pages (Settings > Pages > Deploy from a branch > master,
/docs). No build workflow and no vendored theme: the only files here are the
configuration and the Markdown. `jekyll-seo-tag` and `jekyll-sitemap` are
enabled, which is the point of the exercise.

The module content is moved verbatim. Only the hand-written `<a name="..."/>`
anchors and the section numbering are dropped, both being artefacts of a single
long page, and the cross-references which pointed at them now point at the
pages which replaced them.

Two pages are new:

- "What you would write without spring-addons" names, for each auto-configured
  bean, the Spring Security code it stands for. The trust objection the starter
  README opens with is the most common reason not to adopt these libs, and the
  answer to it was already in the code: almost everything is
  `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, so every default is reversible on its own.
- "Versions and compatibility" carries the spring-addons to Spring Boot table,
  which visitors on an older Boot line need before anything else.

The samples keep their READMEs in the repository, next to the code they
explain, and the site links to them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: ch4mpy
commits.message:
Wire Dependabot on Maven and the GitHub Actions

Nothing watched the build inputs of this repository so far: `ci.yml` still
pinned `actions/checkout@v2`, and dependency bumps only happened when a
release forced the question.

`.github/dependabot.yml` declares two ecosystems, both weekly:

- `maven` on the reactor root, whose `<modules>` Dependabot follows, so the
  starters and the samples are covered by the single entry. Minors and patches
  are grouped into one pull request a week, which is one CI run to read and one
  merge; majors keep a branch of their own.
- `github-actions` on the workflows, grouped the same way.

Three ignore rules keep the proposals meaningful: the samples depend on
spring-addons itself at `${project.version}` and must not be pinned to the
latest release, and the Spring Boot major and the Spring Cloud release train
are release decisions for this project rather than dependency bumps.

Version updates are only half of it: Dependabot alerts and security updates
are repository settings, under Settings > Code security.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: ch4mpy
commits.message:
Publish a GitHub Release for each tag

`mvn release:prepare` pushes 40+ tags so far, none of which had a GitHub
Release: no Releases tab, no feed for watchers, and no notes attached to the
Dependabot PRs bumping spring-addons in other projects, although
`release-notes.md` documents every version.

- `scripts/release-notes.sh` extracts the section of a version from
  `release-notes.md` (`####` module sub-headings included).
- `.github/workflows/release.yml` publishes the Release when the tag is pushed,
  with that section as its body. It checks out the default branch rather than
  the tag, so a manual run can also backfill the Releases of older tags, without
  stealing the "Latest" badge from the current version.
- `release.sh` wraps `mvn clean install release:prepare release:perform` as
  before, sourcing SDKMAN when `sdk` is not in scope, refusing to release a
  version which has no release notes, and bumping the version in the
  documentation snippets beforehand.
- `.gitattributes` keeps `*.sh` with LF endings, which the Ubuntu runner needs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: ch4mpy
commits.message:
Replace samples with five focused modules, fix three bugs they surfaced

The samples and tutorials had grown into a matrix of near-duplicate modules
(servlet/reactive x JWT/introspection x default/OAuthentication) which was
long to read and hard to keep alive. They are replaced by five runnable
applications, each demonstrating one thing, each with a README explaining
what the configuration replaces:

- resource-server (8081): REST API secured with JWT access tokens, security
  configuration entirely in properties, one bean overridden to switch to
  OAuthentication<OpenidToken>, plus an "introspection" profile swapping the
  JWT decoder for token introspection without touching controllers or tests
- resource-server-reactive (8082): the same in WebFlux, with no security
  Java code at all, to show properties and test annotations are unchanged
- bff (8080): OAuth2 BFF, servlet spring-cloud-gateway with oauth2Login and
  TokenRelay=, PKCE, RP-Initiated and Back-Channel Logout, CSRF cookie for
  JavaScript and 2xx OAuth2 redirection statuses for a SPA
- rest-client (8083): RestClient beans auto-configured from properties,
  Bearer forwarded from the security context, Bearer from a
  client_credentials registration, @ImportHttpServices group backed by one
- client-and-resource-server (8084): both auto-configured chains in one
  application, a session-secured Thymeleaf UI redirected to login and a
  stateless API answering 401, the routing decided by client.security-matchers

Tests need neither Docker nor a network: token decoding is mocked and the
consumed APIs are WireMock stubs.

Bugs found while writing them:

- spring-addons-starter-oidc: the resource server auto-configuration was
  gated on Spring Security's HeaderBearerTokenResolver while referencing
  Spring Boot's OAuth2ResourceServerProperties in a bean signature, so an
  application with only the Security jar on its class-path failed to start
  with a NoClassDefFoundError. An OAuth2 client pulling that jar through
  spring-addons-starter-oidc-test was enough to hit it.
- spring-addons-oauth2-test: @WithOidcLogin ignored its nameAttributeKey
  attribute (the DefaultOidcUser was built without it), so getName() always
  returned the sub claim, unlike @WithOAuth2Login.
- spring-addons-starter-oidc README: the FAQ documented the deprecated
  authorization-request-params / token-request-params properties with the
  map syntax of the current ones, which binds to neither, so a copied Auth0
  "audience" parameter was silently dropped. The client filter chain order
  was documented as LOWEST_PRECEDENCE + 1 instead of - 1, and the
  authentication converter sample used a constructor removed in 8.0.0.

Also:
- spring-addons-starter-rest README: document that spring-boot-restclient
  and spring-boot-webclient are optional and must be brought by the app
- root pom: drop the explicit spring-boot-maven-plugin version, which
  resolved to this project's version in grandchild modules
- infra: the realm export now matches the samples (Back-Channel Logout URL
  of spring-addons-user, its 8084 redirect URI, and view-users for the
  spring-addons-m2m service account)

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: ch4mpy
commits.message:
Proxy credentials for HTTPS tunnels with HttpComponents and Jetty

Proxy authentication relied on a Proxy-Authorization header set on each
request, which only reaches the proxy for plain http:// targets (and with the
JDK client, which copies it onto its CONNECT request). For https:// targets,
HttpComponents and Jetty open a CONNECT tunnel first and the proxy's 407 went
unanswered. Credentials are now also registered where these clients look for
them: a CredentialsProvider scoped to the proxy host (HttpComponents) and a
BasicAuthentication for the proxy URI in the AuthenticationStore (Jetty). The
header is kept for the other cases.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.author: ch4mpy
commits.message:
spring-addons-starter-rest: honor https_proxy

Only http_proxy was read and applied to every request. https_proxy is now
bound too (environment variable or https-proxy property): the servlet request
factory routes https:// targets through it and http:// targets through
http_proxy, each falling back to the other when only one is set (a single
underlying client is built when both resolve to the same proxy). Clients which
can't select a proxy per request (WebClient connector, Reactor request factory)
use https_proxy first. Proxy properties (host, port…) keep taking precedence
over both.

SystemProxyProperties gains an httpsProxy field, a getProxyFor(scheme) accessor
and a three-argument constructor; ProxySupport gains a scheme-aware constructor.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
